h: Mud, streams and a proper Cornish breather
p: Cardinham is a valley wood, which gives it a cosy, tucked-away feel. A stream runs along the bottom, and the paths follow the water before climbing up through mixed conifers and broadleaf trees. Little ones love a bit of stick-throwing by the water, while older kids can be sent ahead to find the next waymarker. In late spring, look out for wildflowers along the banks, and in autumn the broadleaf stretches put on a lovely show of colour.

Bikers have plenty to go at, from family-friendly forest roads to steeper, more technical singletrack for confident riders. As always, check the trail grades at the start before anyone heads off, and remember walkers, dogs and riders share some routes, so a friendly bell or shout goes a long way.

Practical tips: wellies or walking boots are a must after rain, because the clue is in the name and the paths do get muddy. Dogs are welcome, so bring a towel for the car. Allow two or three hours for a walk and a cuppa, longer if you are riding.

Cardinham pairs brilliantly with other things to do around Bodmin. Lanhydrock, the National Trust house and estate, is just a short drive away. Bodmin Jail tells the darker side of the town's history, and the Bodmin and Wenford Railway runs heritage trains through the countryside. If you have bikes with you, the Camel Trail sets off from Bodmin towards Wadebridge and Padstow, a flat, traffic-free ride with river views and the promise of a pasty at the end.
